title: AI Literacy Logbook
tagline: Proves your team meets EU AI Act Article 4 with role-based micro-training and an audit-ready record
target_segment: EU SMBs deploying AI tools (Germany, Netherlands, Austria, Ireland first)
problem: Since 2 February 2025 every company that deploys AI systems in the EU, including a 15-person agency using ChatGPT, Copilot or an AI recruiting tool, must take measures to support staff AI literacy under Article 4 of the AI Act. The July 2026 Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) softened the wording to 'take measures to support' rather than guarantee a level, but did not remove the duty. SMB owners do not know which tools count, which roles need what, or how to prove anything if a regulator, client or works council asks. Generic e-learning courses cost EUR 30-100 per seat, are not tied to the tools the firm actually uses, and leave no usable record.
solution: AI Literacy Logbook starts with a 10-minute AI-tool inventory: it reads the company's SaaS list (Google Workspace / Microsoft 365 admin export or a simple form) and an LLM classifies each tool by AI Act role and risk tier. It then generates role-specific 5-minute micro-lessons and quizzes for each tool actually in use (for example 'Copilot in Outlook for sales staff'), delivered by email or Slack/Teams. Completion, quiz results and a dated policy acknowledgement are written into a tamper-evident register that exports as a one-page PDF evidence pack for clients, auditors or works councils. Unlike generic courses it updates automatically when a new AI tool shows up in the inventory, and it keeps one record of which measures were taken for whom, which is what the amended Article 4 asks for.
target_audience: EU SMBs 10-250 staff using generative AI; Marketing and recruitment agencies; IT MSPs reselling to clients; DPOs and external compliance consultants
business_model: Subscription per seat, partner/white-label tier for MSPs and DPO consultancies
pricing: EUR 3 per seat/month (min EUR 29/month); MSP white-label EUR 199/month for 25 client tenants; one-off evidence pack EUR 149
score_justification: L5 AI classifies tools and writes lessons; E4 inventory+LMS-lite in 2 wks; A3 steady Article 4 search interest, softened by Omnibus; P3 MSP/DPO channel and M365 marketplace; M3 tool-to-risk classification library compounds; W3 SMBs buy training but many will do the minimum
platform_distribution: Microsoft AppSource / Teams app; MSP and DPO-consultant partnerships; LinkedIn and German-language SEO ('KI-Kompetenz Nachweis')
tam_source: bottom-up: ~500k EU SMBs actively deploying AI x EUR 300/yr (est.)
competitors: KI-Campus (free courses); Provimedia AI literacy certificates; AhaSlides AI Act course templates; DNV AI literacy training; Generic LMS such as TalentLMS
competitor_gap: Courses are generic and seat-licensed; none build the inventory of tools actually in use or produce a per-tool, per-role evidence record that updates automatically
demand_evidence: Multiple trade and vendor sources (KI-Campus, Provimedia, DPO Consulting) published 2026 explainers that Article 4 remains mandatory after the Omnibus, and the Commission AI Act Service Desk shows Article 4 marked as amended, which shows continuing buyer confusion.
unique_data_capture: Classified library of AI tools mapped to AI Act roles, risk tiers and the training each role needs; improves with every tenant inventory
commoditization_risk: Medium: LMS vendors and Microsoft could add AI-literacy modules, but they will not build per-tenant tool inventories for SMBs
regulatory_notes: Provide compliance tooling, not legal advice; state that the Omnibus wording requires measures, not a guaranteed competence level; GDPR for staff training records

payment_rails: Stripe (cards, SEPA Direct Debit), Paddle as merchant of record for EU VAT
mvp_features: AI-tool inventory import and classification; Role-based micro-lesson generator; Email/Teams delivery and quiz; Evidence register with PDF export; New-tool alert
tech_stack: Next.js + Supabase + LLM API (Claude/GPT) + Microsoft Graph API + Postmark
review_notes: Omnibus softening may reduce urgency; needs German-language content (DE) early since DACH is the most compliance-driven market.

title: Shop Accessibility Fixer
tagline: EAA/BFSG for small shops: exemption test, real code fixes and a compliant accessibility statement
target_segment: Small e-commerce shops selling to EU consumers (Germany, France, Netherlands, Spain), including UK shops selling into the EU
problem: The European Accessibility Act has applied since 28 June 2025 to e-commerce services sold to EU consumers. Germany's BFSG allows fines up to EUR 100,000 and France and Spain have reported first actions. Microenterprises (under 10 staff and at most EUR 2M turnover) are exempt only for services and must document that status, while a shop with 12 staff or one selling covered products is fully in scope. Owners are sold JavaScript overlays that disability groups criticise and that do not fix the underlying theme, or audits costing EUR 2,000+. Independent retail sites had the lowest automated WCAG pass rates in 2026 scans (about 34%, per one unverified industry report).
solution: Shop Accessibility Fixer runs a 3-question exemption test and stores a signed, dated exemption memo if the shop qualifies. For in-scope shops it crawls the storefront and checkout, combines axe-core results with an LLM review of screenshots and DOM (alt text quality, form labels, focus order, contrast, cookie-banner traps), and then produces actual fixes: generated alt text pushed back through the Shopify/WooCommerce API, theme Liquid/CSS patches as pull requests, and a checklist for issues that need human design work. It generates the accessibility information page required by EAA Annex V / BFSG in German, French, Dutch or Spanish with a feedback route, and re-scans monthly. Fixing the source, rather than overlaying it, gives the shop a defensible record if a regulator or complainant asks.
target_audience: Shopify and WooCommerce merchants with 10-50 staff selling to EU consumers; Microenterprises needing an exemption record; Small web agencies serving merchants
business_model: Subscription plus one-off fix packs
pricing: Free exemption test; EUR 39/month monitoring + statement; EUR 299 one-off fix pack; Agency plan EUR 149/month for 15 stores
score_justification: L4 AI writes alt text, patches and statements, some manual design work remains; E4 axe-core+LLM+Shopify API in 2 wks; A4 heavy BFSG/EAA search interest; P5 Shopify App Store and WooCommerce plugin directory; M3 per-theme fix library compounds; W3 merchants pay but overlay prices anchor low
platform_distribution: Shopify App Store; WordPress.org plugin directory; German e-commerce agencies; SEO on 'BFSG Onlineshop'
tam_source: bottom-up: ~250k in-scope EU-facing small shops x EUR 480/yr (est.)
competitors: accessiBe; UserWay; TestParty; Clym; Accesstive
competitor_gap: Overlays do not change source code; audit-led tools are priced for mid-market; none combine exemption documentation, local-language statements and automatic theme fixes for small shops
demand_evidence: 2026 vendor and trade content on EAA fines by country and Shopify obligations is plentiful (Clym, TestParty, Xictron), and an industry first-year report claims BAFA, DGCCRF and Spanish authorities opened first actions against e-commerce checkouts (unverified).

commoditization_risk: Medium: Shopify could ship native checks and overlay vendors are adding AI, but source-level theme patches plus exemption records are a narrower, defensible niche
regulatory_notes: Not legal advice on exemption status; avoid claiming 'fully compliant' since automated checks catch only part of WCAG issues; national transposition rules differ

payment_rails: Shopify Billing API; Stripe for WooCommerce and agencies

tech_stack: Node + Shopify App Bridge + Playwright + axe-core + LLM API (Claude/GPT) vision + Supabase
review_notes: Local-language statements needed (DE/FR/NL/ES); biggest risk is a crowded overlay market and merchants who self-declare as exempt.

title: NIS2 Supplier Answer Desk
tagline: Answers the NIS2 security questionnaires big customers send small suppliers, from one evidence vault
target_segment: Small non-SaaS suppliers to NIS2 entities in Germany, Netherlands and Belgium (logistics, MSPs, manufacturers, facility services)
problem: NIS2 requires essential and important entities to manage supply-chain security, so they push long questionnaires (often 100-300 questions in Excel or a supplier portal) onto every small supplier. A 20-person logistics firm or machine-parts maker has no security team and receives a different format from each customer, each taking 1-3 days of the owner's or IT contractor's time. Getting it wrong risks losing the contract. Tools like Vanta, Conveyor and Loopio target SaaS companies with security teams and five-figure budgets, and the Commission's January 2026 NIS2 simplification proposal shows how confusing scope remains for 6,200+ micro and small firms.
solution: NIS2 Supplier Answer Desk interviews the owner once in plain language (backups, MFA, patching, incident contacts, subcontractors) and collects evidence such as policies, insurance certificates, M365 secure score and screenshots into a vault. When a questionnaire arrives (Excel, PDF or portal copy-paste), an LLM maps each question to the vault and drafts an answer citing the evidence. It flags gaps honestly rather than inventing controls, and returns the file in the customer's format. A gap list ranks the cheapest fixes, for example 'turn on MFA for 3 admin accounts', and generates short policy documents (incident response, access control) the firm actually needs. Each answered questionnaire improves the mapping, so the tenth customer questionnaire takes minutes.
target_audience: Suppliers with 5-100 staff selling to energy, transport, health, manufacturing or digital-infrastructure customers; IT MSPs answering on behalf of clients; Purchasing teams who want suppliers to answer faster
business_model: Subscription with per-questionnaire overage
pricing: EUR 79/month (3 questionnaires/month); EUR 149 per extra questionnaire; MSP plan EUR 349/month for 10 clients
score_justification: L4 AI maps and drafts answers, humans confirm; E4 parsing+RAG in 2 wks; A3 demand is real but spread across firms not searching for 'NIS2'; P2 no built-in channel beyond MSPs; M4 questionnaire-to-control mapping corpus compounds; W3 suppliers pay to protect contracts but budgets are small
platform_distribution: IT MSP partnerships; Chambers of commerce (IHK) cyber events; LinkedIn content for purchasing and supplier managers; Microsoft AppSource
tam_source: bottom-up: ~200k small suppliers to NIS2 entities in DE/NL/BE x EUR 1,000/yr (est.)
competitors: Vanta Questionnaire Automation; Conveyor; Loopio; SafeBase; Excel templates from consultants
competitor_gap: Incumbents assume a security team, SOC 2 evidence and SaaS budgets; none offer plain-language intake, honest gap flagging and a price for 20-person non-software suppliers
demand_evidence: The Commission's NIS2 page notes the January 2026 targeted amendments meant to ease compliance for 28,700 companies, including 6,200 micro and small enterprises; Vanta and Conveyor both advertise questionnaire automation, showing proven spend in the larger segment.
unique_data_capture: Corpus of real NIS2 supplier questionnaires by customer and sector mapped to normalised controls; lets the product pre-answer new customers' forms and benchmark supplier maturity
commoditization_risk: Medium: Vanta/Conveyor could move down-market and general AI assistants can fill spreadsheets, but evidence vault plus mapping corpus plus price point give a defensible niche
regulatory_notes: Answers are the supplier's attestations; product must not invent controls (liability for misrepresentation); GDPR for evidence documents; not legal advice on NIS2 scope

payment_rails: Stripe (cards, SEPA Direct Debit), invoice billing for MSPs
mvp_features: Plain-language security intake; Evidence vault; Questionnaire import (xlsx/pdf) and AI answer mapping; Gap list with fix guide; Policy document generator; Export in customer format
tech_stack: Next.js + Postgres/pgvector + LLM API (Claude/GPT) + openpyxl/docx tooling + EU-region hosting
review_notes: German and Dutch UI and answers needed (DE/NL); key risk is Vanta-style vendors moving down-market. Distinct from corpus IDEA-003 (SOC 2 automation for SaaS) because it serves non-SaaS suppliers answering inbound forms.

title: Small Firm DSAR Desk
tagline: UK subject access requests for small employers: mailbox search, AI redaction, deadline tracking
target_segment: UK SMBs and charities with 10-250 staff, especially employers facing DSARs from departing or disputing employees
problem: UK employers increasingly receive subject access requests from staff in grievances or tribunal claims, and responding means searching years of email, Teams chats and HR files and redacting third-party data within one month. A 40-person firm can spend 20-60 staff hours or GBP 2,000-10,000 in solicitor fees on one request (est.). The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 added rules on time limits and 'reasonable and proportionate' searches, which helps only if the firm can show how it searched. Enterprise privacy platforms such as Transcend and OneTrust target large consumer brands, not a dental group or a recruitment agency facing an angry ex-employee.
solution: Small Firm DSAR Desk logs the request, computes the statutory deadline (including clarification pauses) and walks the user through identity checks. It connects to Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace via read-only APIs, runs a scoped search across mail, chat and shared drives, and records the search parameters as a proportionality log under the DUAA search provisions. An LLM then classifies every hit (personal data of the requester, third-party data, legally privileged material, irrelevant) and proposes redactions, which a human approves in a fast review screen. It assembles the response pack with a covering letter and the supplementary information Article 15 requires. Fixed pricing per request makes it far cheaper than solicitor review and gives the firm a defensible audit trail if the ICO or a tribunal asks.
target_audience: UK SMB owners and HR managers; Outsourced HR consultants; Small law firms doing employment defence; Schools and charities
business_model: Per-request pricing plus optional annual subscription
pricing: GBP 249 per request (up to 5,000 items); GBP 99/month subscription incl. 1 request/quarter; HR-consultant plan GBP 299/month
score_justification: L4 AI classifies and redacts, human signs off; E3 M365/Google connectors + review UI take 2-3 wks; A4 employee DSARs are a constant UK HR pain; P2 sells through HR consultants, no marketplace pull; M3 redaction feedback improves classifiers; W5 firms already pay solicitors thousands per DSAR
platform_distribution: Outsourced HR consultancies and employment-law firms as resellers; Microsoft AppSource; SEO for 'respond to subject access request employee'
tam_source: bottom-up: ~150k UK employer DSARs/yr (est.) x GBP 400 average spend
competitors: Transcend DSR Automation; MineOS; OneTrust; Employment solicitors (manual review); Microsoft Purview eDiscovery
competitor_gap: Enterprise tools focus on consumer data held in many systems and cost five figures; Purview needs E5 licences and expertise; solicitors are slow and expensive
demand_evidence: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 adds dedicated sections on DSAR time limits and searches (ss.76 and 78), which changes how firms must run searches; enterprise vendors like Transcend and MineOS sell DSR automation, showing proven willingness to pay further up-market.
unique_data_capture: Labelled corpus of SMB email/chat redaction decisions (third-party, privileged, irrelevant) that sharpens classification accuracy over time
commoditization_risk: Medium: Microsoft Purview and Copilot could add DSAR workflows for E5 customers, but SMB plans lack them and the proportionality log is product-specific
regulatory_notes: Processes highly sensitive personal data, so the firm must be the data processor under a DPA with UK-hosted storage; legal-advice risk on exemptions (privilege, management forecasting), so flag for lawyer review; ICO registration

payment_rails: Stripe (cards, Bacs Direct Debit via GoCardless)
mvp_features: Request log + deadline calculator; M365/Google read-only search; AI classification and redaction review; Proportionality search log; Response pack generator
tech_stack: Next.js + Postgres + Microsoft Graph / Google Workspace APIs + LLM API (Claude/GPT) + PDF redaction library, UK-region hosting
review_notes: Trust and security certification is the gating risk; a single data leak would end the business.

title: EU E-Invoice Bridge
tagline: Lets UK suppliers send the Peppol/Factur-X e-invoices their Belgian, French and German buyers demand
target_segment: UK and other non-EU SMB suppliers invoicing B2B customers in Belgium, France and Germany
problem: EU countries are moving to mandatory structured e-invoicing: Belgium's Peppol B2B mandate from January 2026, France's reception obligation for all VAT-registered businesses from 1 September 2026, Poland's KSeF from February/April 2026 and Germany's reception duty since 2025. UK freelancers, agencies and manufacturers sending PDF invoices from Xero, QuickBooks or Word increasingly get them rejected by EU accounts-payable teams or paid late. Their UK software does not issue Peppol BIS or Factur-X, and EU access-point providers sell to local companies in local languages with onboarding built for larger volumes.
solution: EU E-Invoice Bridge lets a supplier forward or upload their existing PDF invoice, or connect Xero, QuickBooks or FreeAgent. An LLM extracts the invoice data, validates it against the destination country's rules (buyer VAT ID, reverse-charge wording, purchase-order reference, Leitweg-ID for German public buyers), and converts it to Peppol BIS 3.0, XRechnung or Factur-X. It is then sent through a certified Peppol access point partner, or emailed as a valid hybrid file where that is accepted. It tracks delivery and rejection messages, explains rejections in plain English and suggests the fix. Buyer-specific requirements learned from each rejection are remembered, so the second invoice to the same customer goes through first time.

pricing: GBP 12/month (20 invoices); GBP 39/month (150 invoices); Bookkeeper plan GBP 99/month for 20 clients

competitor_gap: Access-point providers are API-first or enterprise-led, priced and supported for EU domestic companies; none target UK exporters with PDF-in, plain-English rejection handling

title: Plateforme Agréée Migrator
tagline: Moves French accountants' small clients onto e-invoicing before the September 2027 issuing deadline
target_segment: French accounting firms (cabinets d'expertise comptable) and their TPE/PME clients in France
problem: Since 1 September 2026 every VAT-registered French business must be able to receive e-invoices via a plateforme agréée (PA), and SMEs and micro-enterprises must start issuing them and e-reporting by 1 September 2027. A typical cabinet has 200-800 small clients, each invoicing from a different tool (Word, Excel, Sumup, sector software) with unknown e-reporting needs for B2C or international sales. Partners must audit each client, recommend a PA and track readiness, all while busy season lasts until May. Doing this by phone and spreadsheet costs an estimated 1-2 hours per client.
solution: Plateforme Agréée Migrator sends each client a short French questionnaire and asks for three sample sales invoices. An LLM reads the samples and the client's FEC (fichier des écritures comptables) export to classify invoicing flows (domestic B2B, B2C, intra-EU, export), detect missing mandatory mentions (SIREN, delivery address, transaction category) and estimate e-reporting obligations. It scores readiness and recommends a migration path (stay on the cabinet's PA, switch invoicing tool, or connect the existing tool), then generates a personalised lettre de mission addendum and client email. The firm gets a dashboard of all clients by status and deadline, with automated reminders. It turns a manual audit into a batch process and creates a billable advisory service for the cabinet.

title: CBAM Threshold Guard
tagline: Tracks your steel, aluminium and fertiliser imports against the 50-tonne CBAM threshold before you cross it
target_segment: Small EU importers and customs brokers in Germany, Netherlands, Italy, Poland and Ireland
problem: CBAM's definitive period started on 1 January 2026 with a single 50-tonne annual mass threshold per importer. Below it, a small firm importing fasteners, aluminium profiles or fertiliser is exempt. Once it crosses it, obligations apply to the whole year's imports, including goods brought in before, and importing above the threshold without authorised-declarant status is penalised. Small importers and their brokers track tonnage across many customs declarations, CN codes and brokers, often in Excel, and have no early warning. CBAM software vendors target heavy industry and emissions data collection, not the threshold watch that thousands of small importers need.
solution: CBAM Threshold Guard ingests customs declarations (broker CSV/PDF exports, ATLAS/AGS/AIDA exports) and uses an LLM plus a CN-code table to flag CBAM-relevant lines, including downstream products like screws and bolts that importers often miss. It sums net mass per legal entity on a rolling calendar-year basis and forecasts when the 50-tonne threshold will be hit from the order pipeline. It alerts the importer and their broker at 60%, 80% and 95%. For firms likely to cross, it pre-fills the authorised-declarant application data and starts supplier emissions-data requests in the supplier's language. For firms staying below, it stores a year-end evidence file showing they stayed under the threshold.

pricing: EUR 49/month per importer; Broker plan EUR 399/month for 30 importers; Supplier data request pack EUR 25 per supplier

platform_distribution: Customs broker partnerships; Trade associations (e.g. fastener wholesale groups); LinkedIn and German/Dutch SEO on 'CBAM Schwellenwert 50 Tonnen'
tam_source: bottom-up: ~70k EU importers of CBAM goods near the threshold x EUR 600/yr (est.)

competitor_gap: CBAM platforms focus on embedded-emissions calculation for large declarants; nobody offers cheap, broker-integrated threshold forecasting and below-threshold evidence for small importers
demand_evidence: National authorities (Finnish Customs, Malta) warn small importers that imports can be blocked in 2026 and that crossing 50 tonnes makes the whole year's imports subject to CBAM, a clear early-warning need.
unique_data_capture: Declaration-line classification of CBAM goods plus a growing supplier emissions-data directory (installation-level values from Asian and Turkish producers)
commoditization_risk: Low: the niche is too small for big CBAM vendors and requires broker data integration that general AI assistants lack

mvp_features: Declaration import (CSV/PDF); CBAM CN-code flagging incl. downstream goods; Rolling tonnage + forecast; Threshold alerts to importer and broker; Declarant application pre-fill; Supplier emissions request generator

title: EUDR Small Operator Kit
tagline: Gets micro and small importers of coffee, cocoa, wood and rubber EUDR-ready for the June 2027 deadline
target_segment: Micro and small operators and traders in the EU (Germany, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy) importing EUDR commodities
problem: The EUDR was postponed again by Regulation (EU) 2025/2650: it now applies from 30 December 2026 for large and medium operators and from 30 June 2027 for micro and small operators, with a simplified one-time declaration replacing repeated due-diligence statements for some small primary operators. Specialty coffee roasters, chocolate makers and furniture importers face shifting rules and large customers demanding geolocation data now. They cannot tell whether they count as operators or traders, which simplification applies, or how to collect plot polygons from smallholder cooperatives. Enterprise traceability platforms cost EUR 10k+ a year.
solution: EUDR Small Operator Kit begins with a role and date classifier: based on company size, product HS codes and supply chain position it tells the user whether they are an operator, downstream operator or trader, whether micro or small simplifications apply, and the exact date that applies. It then sends suppliers and cooperatives a multilingual WhatsApp/web form to collect plot coordinates or polygons. AI cleans the geodata and checks it against public deforestation layers (e.g. JRC forest maps, Global Forest Watch), and the kit assembles a risk-assessment file and simplified declaration ready for the EU Information System. Buyer-facing exports satisfy the large retailers already asking for data.

demand_evidence: The European Commission's EUDR page lists separate dates for micro and small operators (30 June 2027), and law-firm and vendor commentary (Jones Day, VinciWorks, Tanso) shows repeated confusion over the delayed and simplified rules.
